public_rationale: The preprint submitted September 26, 2025, reports library hallucinations in generated code and examines their sensitivity to prompt variations [e1]. Its supplied abstract does not jointly compare functional failures and hallucination rates across independently measured levels of coding-task complexity [e1]. It establishes that library hallucinations occur, but does not settle the claimed increase in failures and hallucinations as tasks become more complex [e1].
limitations: Prompt variations are not established here as a measure of engineering-task complexity [e1].
The supplied record does not specify experimental dates, so publication in September does not establish performance during September 1–29, 2025 [e1].
The library-hallucination results do not establish a corresponding trend in functional failures [e1].

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Coding LLMs can generate code but break down and hallucinate more as tasks get more complex.

statement.excerpt: In reality, LLMs can generate code, and do some software engineering-adjacent tasks, but, like all Large Language Models, break down and go totally insane, hallucinating more as the tasks get more complex.

from_speaker: hallucinating more as the tasks get more complex
our_interpretation: Read the rhetorical description of breakdown as declining functional reliability, and hallucination as invented or unsupported code elements or factual assertions.
The ordinary reading predicts increasing failure and hallucination rates as coding tasks become more demanding.
No reporting period is specified. Use September 1–29, 2025, the latest calendar month observable before publication, for the ongoing capability claim; earlier studies provide context.
Task complexity must be measured independently of whether the model failed. Task duration, dependencies and required changes are possible measures, not definitions supplied by Zitron.
criteria.support_condition: Comparable evaluations of contemporary coding models show that both failures and separately measured hallucinations increase across independently defined levels of task complexity.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable evaluations show reliable performance and stable or declining hallucination rates as complexity increases across a representative task range.
